bioghist.head: Biographical / Historical
bioghist.p: This collection primarily contains haggadot (singular: haggadah) from the Yishuv and the State of Israel. A haggadah is the text that is recited at the Passover seder. The traditional text was largely standardized by the Middle Ages, and it was frequently reproduced in both manuscript and print throughout the centuries.

In the 20th century, various Jewish groups decided to change the text for their own religious or political purposes. This phenomenon was especially prevalent on kibbutzim (singular: kibbutz), collective communities in the Yishuv and in the State of Israel. The leaders of the kibbutzim recognized the power of the Passover seder and the redemption narrative in the effort to create their own national narrative, as well as the power of a collective communal performance of a ritual. The text of the haggadah thus became a vehicle for creativity and identity-formation.

Hundreds of kibbutz haggadot were created, with over 500 editions between 1930 and 1960, and they were each slightly different. The themes of spring, agriculture, and working the land were prominently featured, drawing on both biblical verses as well as medieval and contemporary Hebrew poetry. Another prominent theme was the exile in and subsequent exodus from Egypt. While this theme is central in the traditional text, these haggadot removed the rabbinic texts that traditionally told the story and replaced them with excerpts from the biblical book of Exodus, highlighting Moses's role in the redemption and often removing God from any part of the story. These kibbutz haggadot then located their current historical moment in the arc of Jewish history, often describing contemporary historical events in Biblical Hebrew and relaying their own experience moving from slavery or persecution to freedom. They incorporated modern Hebrew literature and poetry from writers such as Hayyim Nahman Bialik (1873-1934), Saul Tchernichowsky (1875-1943), Hannah Senesh (1921-1944), Nathan Alterman (1910-1970), and others. Descriptions of or references to World War II, the Holocaust, the establishment of the State of Israel, and subsequent wars are all common, and capture the specific historical moment the authors were experiencing.

The texts are often, though not always, beautifully illustrated, in a variety of styles. Earlier haggadot were created using mimeography or offset lithography, while later they were professionally printed and illustrated.

Kibbutzim were mostly socialist and secular in nature, with an emphasis on the value of labor, agriculture, and the return of the Jews to the land of Israel. Their communities functioned as participatory democracies. Within the kibbutz movement, there were differing political affiliations, social characters, and religious outlooks, and these contributed to an ever-changing landscape of federations of different groups of kibbutzim. Kibbutzim and their residents contributed significantly to pre-State and Israeli society, economy, culture, politics, and security.

The Yishuv refers to the Jewish population living in Palestine before the State of Israel was established in 1948. This includes the Jewish population under both Ottoman control before World War I and under Mandatory British control after World War I until 1948.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: The Kibbutz and Ephemeral Haggadot from Israel and the Yishuv Collection [1937-1979] contains haggadot (singular: haggadah), the text that is recited at the Passover seder, from the Yishuv and the State of Israel. Most are from kibbutzim from the Yishuv and from Israel, though some are from other organizations such as larger kibbutz movements, newspapers, the military, etc. They span the years 1937-1979, with 2/3 of them from the 1940s and 1950s. All are in Hebrew except one which is in Yiddish. Most of them are illustrated. The collection also includes one songbook that contains songs for Passover and was intended to supplement the accompanying haggadah from that year. These ephemeral haggadot were intended to be used for one year alone, as the kibbutzim would issue new ones each year.

arrangement.head: Arrangement
arrangement.p: The folders are arranged alphabetically according to the Hebrew alphabet by name of kibbutz or publishing institution. The name of the kibbutz or publishing institution is indicated in both the vernacular Hebrew script and the transliterated form.

processinfo.head: Processing Information
processinfo.p: Collections are processed to a variety of levels, depending on the work necessary to make them usable, their perceived research value, the availability of staff, competing priorities, and whether or not further accruals are expected. The library attempts to provide a basic level of preservation and access for all collections, and does more extensive processing of higher priority collections as time and resources permit. These materials have been arranged and described according to national and local standards. For more information, please refer to the Yale Archival Processing Manual.
